root_cause.text: The ntfs3 journal-replay file-record validator in `check_file_record()` failed to validate the on-disk `rec->used` field, so later `do_action()` memmove size calculations could underflow in `fs/ntfs3/fslog.c` and copy excessive data into a 4 KB buffer.
root_cause.evidence: The patch adds `u32 used = le32_to_cpu(rec->used);` and rejects records when `used > rs || used < ao`, plus an extra check that `used` must cover the walked attribute end marker because “the do_action() handlers compute memmove lengths as `rec->used - <offset of validated attr>`, which underflows when `rec->used` is smaller than the attribute walk reached.”

intent_record.intent_summary: Tighten NTFS file record validation by rejecting records with inconsistent used-size bounds.
intent_record.what: The function `check_file_record()` now reads `rec->used` into a new local variable `used`, and the header validation condition was expanded to reject records when `used > rs` or `used < ao` in addition to the existing signature, size, offset, and total-size checks.
intent_record.how: At runtime, file records whose reported used-byte count is larger than the record size or smaller than the attribute offset will now be treated as invalid and rejected earlier, preventing malformed or inconsistent MFT records from being accepted.

intent_record.intent_summary: Add a bounds check in file record validation to prevent memmove length underflow in do_action() handlers.
intent_record.what: A new validation block was inserted in check_file_record() before returning true. It adds a comment explaining a memmove length underflow risk in do_action() handlers, and a guard that returns false when `used < PtrOffset(rec, attr) + sizeof(attr->type)`.
intent_record.how: At runtime, this rejects file records whose reported used size does not extend far enough to cover the ATTR_END marker reached by the attribute walk. That prevents later memmove length calculations from underflowing when they compute `rec->used - <validated attr offset>`, avoiding invalid memory movement and potential corruption or crashes.
